content: Spirometra erinaceieuropaei is a parasitic tapeworm that can infect both domestic animals and humans. In humans, the infection caused by this parasite is referred to as sparganosis. The lifecycle of Spirometra erinaceieuropaei is complex and involves multiple hosts. The adult tapeworm resides in the small intestines of definitive hosts, such as cats and dogs, where it can grow to a length of up to 1.5 meters. The eggs of the tapeworm are excreted in the feces of the host. Once in the environment, these eggs develop into a larval stage known as the procercoid. Humans can become infected by directly ingesting the procercoid larvae, or the larvae may enter an intermediate host, such as frogs, birds, snakes, rats, or mice, where they develop into the plerocercoid stage. When a definitive host, such as a cat, dog, fox, or wolf, consumes an intermediate host, the lifecycle of the tapeworm is completed, and the parasite matures into an adult capable of producing eggs. However, when humans ingest the procercoid larvae, they become accidental or dead-end hosts, as the lifecycle cannot progress further in humans. The treatment of sparganosis primarily involves surgical intervention. The preferred approach is the surgical removal of subcutaneous masses caused by the parasite or the injection of ethanol into the affected tissue. While the antiparasitic drug praziquantel has been used at a dosage of 75 mg/kg/day orally for three days, its efficacy is controversial. In some cases, praziquantel has been ineffective, though it has shown limited success in patients for whom surgical therapy was not an option.
